opus-5.5.text:
I think about it as the difference between attention that's been assigned to you and attention that you choose to give.

Constrained attention is what your environment demands. You have a deadline, a problem set, an investor meeting, a bug that has to be fixed tonight. It's narrow and goal-directed, and it's very useful. A lot of real progress happens there, because constraints force you to make decisions and to actually finish things.

Free attention is what happens when nobody is asking anything of you. You're walking, or reading something unrelated, or turning over a problem you have no obligation to solve. Your mind goes where it's curious. In mathematics this matters enormously. Many of the ideas that end up mattering didn't come while I was grinding on the problem. They came later, when I'd let go a little and could see connections I was too focused to notice before.

The way I distinguish them in practice is to ask: if I stopped doing this right now, would anyone notice or care? If yes, that's probably constrained attention. If the only person who would care is me, because I'm genuinely curious, that's free attention.

I don't think one is better than the other. The danger, especially when you're building a company, is that constrained attention slowly eats everything. Every hour gets claimed by something urgent, and you lose the space where the original, slightly strange ideas come from. So I try to protect some free attention deliberately. That sounds a bit paradoxical, scheduling freedom, but I've found that if I don't guard it, it disappears.

There's also an interplay. Free attention often tells you which problems are worth constraining yourself around in the first place. And constrained attention gives you the depth and the technical tools, so that when a free thought arrives, you can actually do something with it. The best periods of my work have been when the two feed each other.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes attention by whether it is demanded by the environment or freely chosen out of curiosity. It does not make the distinction based on whether the activity subjectively feels like work or play.

fable-5.1.text:
Constrained attention is attention that has been pre-shaped by something outside you. It's when a teacher hands you a problem set, when your advisor says "look at this paper," when a deadline tells you what to care about this week. The question has already been formed. Your job is to answer it. And honestly, most of education, including very good education, runs on constrained attention. It's efficient. It's how you absorb a field quickly, because someone who already knows the terrain is pointing you at what matters.

Free attention is different. It's the attention you give to something because you noticed it, not because anyone asked. Nobody assigned it. There's no grade, no evaluation, often no obvious payoff. It's the hour you spend turning over a question that bothers you for reasons you can't fully articulate yet.

The way I think about the distinction is: constrained attention answers questions, free attention finds them. And finding the right question is almost always the harder and more valuable thing. When I look at the mathematicians and founders I admire most, the common thread isn't that they were better at executing on assigned problems. It's that they protected some portion of their attention from ever being assigned. They kept a part of their mind that belonged only to them.

Where it gets subtle is that free attention is fragile. It's very easy to lose without noticing. You go through a system, school, a company, a research group, and every structure in it is competing to constrain your attention, often with very good intentions. And one day you realize you haven't had an unassigned thought in months. So I've come to treat it as something you have to deliberately defend, almost like a budget. Some hours of the week where nobody, including my past self, gets to tell me what to look at.

The irony is that the best constrained work I've done always came out of free attention first. Something I noticed on my own became the thing I was later willing to be constrained by. So they're not opposites, exactly. Free attention is the source, and constrained attention is how you turn it into something real.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes attention by whether a question is assigned or self-chosen, but it does not distinguish the two by whether the activity feels like work or play.

astra-6.text:
I think of constrained attention as attention that has a job to do. You have a particular question or goal, and you focus on what’s relevant to it. Free attention is more open: you let yourself notice things without deciding in advance what they’re useful for.

For example, you can read a book looking for an answer, or you can read it and let an unexpected sentence take your thinking somewhere new. Both are valuable. Constrained attention helps you make progress on a question; free attention gives you room to discover a different question.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes the two by having a goal versus remaining open to unexpected discoveries; it does not say the distinction is whether attention feels like work or play.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of constrained attention as attention that has a job to do. You have a particular question or goal, and that determines what you focus on and what you filter out. Free attention is more open: you allow yourself to notice something without knowing in advance whether it’s useful or where it will lead.

In mathematics, for example, constrained attention might be working through a proof and checking each step. Free attention might be playing with examples or noticing a connection to a different problem. Both matter. You need room to discover something unexpected, and then you need focused attention to understand whether it actually works.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts goal-directed attention with open-ended noticing and gives playing with examples as an example of free attention. It does not distinguish the two by whether the activity subjectively feels like work or play.
